beliefs.practice: Read the cluster connection string from an environment variable (DOCUMENTDB_URI) at runtime, never commit or log the raw connection string; for production store the secret in Azure Key Vault and fetch at startup.

Use a pooled MongoDB driver connection with explicit pool sizing (set maxPoolSize and optionally minPoolSize) and application name; choose pool size appropriate to expected concurrency (e.g., maxPoolSize: 50 for a typical server) and reuse that single client for the app lifetime rather than creating per-request connections.

Handle transient errors and rate-limiting with retries and exponential backoff; detect HTTP 429 / MongoServerSelection/network errors and honor any Retry-After header, with a capped exponential backoff and jitter.

Persist change-stream resume tokens (resumeAfter) durably (e.g., in a collection) and on clean shutdown, then on restart resume the change stream from the last saved token to avoid losing or reprocessing events.

When opening a change stream for updates that need the current document state include fullDocument: 'updateLookup' (or fetch the document in your handler) so you can compute deltas reliably for summary updates.

Implement ward-summary updates as single-document atomic updates using findOneAndUpdate with $inc/$set and upsert: true (avoid multi-document transactions); compute the incremental delta from the change-stream event and apply that delta to the per-ward summary document.
Keep the live ward summary small and single-document-per-ward (partition by wardId) so counters can be updated atomically without transactions and to minimize RU cost of updates.

Create an index on the fields used by frequent queries, e.g., a compound index { wardId: 1, status: 1 } to support queries listing beds per ward by status, and an index { wardId:1, updatedAt:-1 } to support fetching most-recent updates per ward.

Use a TTL index for automatic expiry of cleaning-state documents: create an index on a Date field like cleaningUntil with expireAfterSeconds: 0 and set cleaningUntil to the timestamp when the doc should expire; do not assume immediate deletion — TTL deletion is background-driven and can be delayed.

Design change-stream event handling to be idempotent: persist processed event ids or incorporate idempotency keys so repeated delivery or replays (after resume) do not cause double-counting in ward summaries.

Do not rely on multi-document transactions for per-ward counters; prefer single-document atomic updates or an aggregation pipeline update (findOneAndUpdate with update pipeline) to derive new counter values when necessary.

Monitor RU (request unit) consumption and provisioned throughput; run explain() on heavy queries and add/adjust indexes or increase throughput if you hit 429s for read/write patterns from the demo or API endpoints.

Restrict network access using the database firewall / VNet / private endpoints and avoid opening the cluster to 0.0.0.0/0; when using connection strings in CI/CD use ephemeral credentials and rotate them regularly.

Use application-level schema validation (Mongoose schemas or MongoDB JSON Schema validators) to ensure bed documents include required fields (bedId, wardId, status, updatedAt, cleaningUntil) and to prevent malformed documents that break change-stream logic.

Persist resume tokens and (optionally) last-processed change stream event timestamps in the same cluster (a dedicated control collection) so the watcher can be restarted without external state; ensure those control docs are small and indexed by watcher id.

When using Mongoose, prefer opening native driver change streams (collection.watch) for lower-level control of fullDocument, resume tokens, and errors, or ensure you access the underlying driver stream if you need advanced options.

For vector fields, store the vector as a numeric array in a dedicated field and create a vector index with the vendor-specific index type (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN) and explicit parameters (dimension, metric, M/efConstruction, or indexOptions) matching the runtime queries; test nearest-neighbor queries with explain to validate index usage.
Avoid returning raw database errors to clients; map database error codes (including 429) to user-friendly HTTP responses and include guidance about retry/backoff for rate-limited endpoints.

Use explain() and server-side profiling to find slow operations (especially change-stream processing and aggregation on ward summaries) and add indexes or restructure queries to be covered where possible (project only needed fields).

Expect and handle eventual consistency and out-of-order visibility in distributed change delivery: design summary updates and reads to tolerate short windows where a recently-updated bed may not yet be reflected by a TTL deletion or an index update.

If you need deterministic immediate deletion semantics for cleaning-state docs, do not rely solely on TTL indexes — implement an explicit scheduled job (or set a background worker) to delete expired cleaning docs at the exact time you require.
Instrument and log RU consumption per operation and include request metrics (latency, status) in monitoring so you can correlate API usage patterns with RU spikes and tune throughput accordingly.

Be conservative with index creation: avoid unnecessary indexes (each index increases RU cost on writes); create the minimal set required for your API queries and test with realistic workloads before adding more.

Use optimistic concurrency where useful: include an updatedAt timestamp or a version field in the ward summary document and use conditional updates to detect conflicting concurrent writers if your business logic needs it.

For local developer environments include a .env.example with a placeholder DOCUMENTDB_URI and instruct developers to not commit real credentials; in CI use environment secrets or Key Vault integration to supply the real connection string at runtime.
